name: The Alexander Graham Bell
description: This corner pub occupies a pair of classic Georgian townhouses on George Street dating from around 1785, though a carved lintel over one doorway carries a much older inscription: "God bless the baxters of Edinburgh who built this house 1675", a reference to the city's medieval baker's guild and a much earlier building on the site. The premises traded for years as the Ivory Lounge before JD Wetherspoon took it over in May 2010, renaming it in honour of the world-famous inventor said to have been born just around the corner.
interesting_fact: Alexander Graham Bell, inventor of the telephone, was born at 16 South Charlotte Street - a walk of only a few minutes from this pub's front door, and this tour's own route passes his birthplace separately elsewhere on leg 3. Bell emigrated to Canada and then the United States as a young man, patented the telephone in 1876 while teaching at Boston University, and kept his ties to his native city throughout his life, returning on visits and eventually being made a Freeman of Edinburgh in 1920, over four decades after the invention that made him famous.

name: The Cambridge Bar
description: This two-storey Georgian corner bar on Young Street has become known across Edinburgh for its craft beer selection and gourmet burgers, made with locally-sourced ingredients and served in an L-shaped downstairs bar full of wooden alcoves, low tables and leather benches, with an upstairs room used for private functions and overflow dining. Young Street itself was originally laid out as the westernmost stretch of Thistle Street before being renamed after an early New Town developer - one of the many quiet service lanes tucked just behind George Street's grander frontages.
interesting_fact: The Cambridge Bar shares Young Street with an even more famous neighbour just a few doors along: the Oxford Bar, the unpretentious real-ale pub made internationally known as detective John Rebus's regular haunt in Ian Rankin's bestselling crime novels. The two pubs, named after Britain's oldest rival universities, sit on the same short Edinburgh lane by coincidence rather than design - though it makes for a natural point of comparison between the Oxford's famously spartan, traditional interior and the Cambridge's more contemporary craft-beer-and-burgers approach.
